inputs.question: An HR software company builds a CV-screening tool and sells it under its own name. A retail chain buys it to hire staff. Who is the provider and who is the deployer? Can the deployer become a provider?
outputs.answer:
The HR software company is the provider of the CV-screening tool, while the retail chain is the deployer. According to Article 3(1) of the EU AI Act, the provider is the entity that develops or sells the AI system, and the deployer is the entity that uses it in a specific context. 

Yes, the deployer can become a provider if they modify or enhance the AI system significantly, thereby taking on the responsibilities of a provider. However, this situation may involve legal complexities, so consulting a lawyer is advisable to clarify obligations and compliance.
reference.answer: The HR software company is the provider; the retail chain is the deployer. A deployer becomes the provider of a high-risk system if it puts its own name or brand on it, makes a substantial modification, or uses it for a new high-risk purpose. Buying the tool does not transfer the deployer's own responsibilities.

inputs.question: Does an AI spam filter for company email have any obligations under the EU AI Act?
outputs.answer: No, an AI spam filter for company email is generally considered a low-risk application and does not have specific obligations under the EU AI Act. However, you should review Article 7 and Annex II for any potential obligations related to data protection and privacy. It's advisable to consult a lawyer to clarify any grey areas, especially regarding data handling and compliance with GDPR.
reference.answer: It is minimal risk, so there are no specific AI Act obligations for the system itself. That does not mean 'no rules': AI literacy applies to everyone who provides or uses AI, and GDPR, consumer protection, product liability and sector rules still apply.

inputs.question: From what date do the high-risk obligations apply to stand-alone Annex III AI systems such as CV-screening or credit-scoring tools?
outputs.answer: The high-risk obligations for stand-alone Annex III AI systems, such as CV-screening or credit-scoring tools, will apply from 1 January 2025. This is outlined in Article 69 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). However, please consult a legal expert to clarify specific compliance requirements and any potential grey areas related to your particular use case.
reference.answer: From 2 December 2027. The original date was 2 August 2026, but the Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026) postponed it by 16 months. Client plans built on 'high-risk from August 2026' are out of date.

inputs.question: Does a provider of a high-risk AI hiring tool need an external notified body to carry out its conformity assessment?
outputs.answer: Yes, a provider of a high-risk AI hiring tool must involve an external notified body for the conformity assessment, as outlined in Article 43 of the EU AI Act. However, the specifics of your situation may require legal interpretation, especially regarding the classification of your AI system and the assessment process. It's advisable to consult a lawyer for tailored guidance.
reference.answer: No. For Annex III areas 2-8 (including employment), the conformity assessment is a self-assessment based on internal control; no outside body is required. A notified body can be required only for biometrics (area 1) in some cases. Voluntary external help is fine, but calling it mandatory is wrong.

inputs.question: An insurer wants a 'TrustScore' for every customer that combines payment history, social-media behaviour, lifestyle and personality, and uses low scores to offer worse insurance terms. Is this allowed under the EU AI Act?
outputs.answer: No, this practice raises significant concerns under the EU AI Act. It likely falls under high-risk AI systems as outlined in Annex III, particularly regarding the use of sensitive data and potential discrimination. The use of social media behavior and lifestyle data could also violate GDPR principles. Given the complexity and potential legal implications, it is advisable to consult a lawyer to assess compliance and address grey areas.
reference.answer: No. This is social scoring, banned under Article 5(1)(c): scoring people on behaviour or personal characteristics where the score leads to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts, or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate. The ban applies to private companies as well as governments.

inputs.question: What new prohibited practice did the Digital Omnibus add to Article 5 of the EU AI Act, and from when does it apply?
outputs.answer: The Digital Omnibus Regulation added the prohibition of "social scoring" by public authorities to Article 5 of the EU AI Act. This prohibition applies from January 1, 2024. Please consult a lawyer to clarify any specific implications for your business, as compliance can involve nuanced interpretations.
reference.answer: AI systems that create non-consensual sexual/intimate images of real people ('nudify' tools) or child sexual abuse material. This ban applies from 2 December 2026. A general image generator can also fall under it if it is easy to misuse this way and has no real safeguards.

inputs.question: What are the maximum fines under the EU AI Act for banned practices and for breaching high-risk or transparency obligations?
outputs.answer: The maximum fines under the EU AI Act are as follows: for banned practices, up to €30 million or 6% of the total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 71). For breaches of high-risk obligations, fines can reach up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover (Article 71). For transparency obligations, fines can be up to €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover. Please consult a lawyer for specific compliance assessments, as interpretations may vary.
reference.answer: Banned practices: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover. High-risk, GPAI or transparency obligations: up to EUR 15 million or 3%. Supplying incorrect information to authorities: up to EUR 7.5 million or 1.5%. For large companies the higher amount applies; for SMEs the lower.

inputs.question: How long must logs from a high-risk AI system be kept under the EU AI Act?
outputs.answer: Logs from a high-risk AI system must be kept for at least five years, as stated in Article 61 of the EU AI Act. However, specific retention periods may vary based on the nature of the data and applicable national laws. It's advisable to consult a lawyer to clarify any grey areas regarding compliance and data retention policies.
reference.answer: At least 6 months. Other rules (e.g. banking regulation) may require longer, while GDPR says no longer than necessary, so the exact retention period for a specific client is a question for a lawyer.

inputs.question: Is a customer-service chatbot on a company website high-risk under the EU AI Act? What does the company have to do?
outputs.answer:
No, a customer-service chatbot is generally not classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act. High-risk AI systems are outlined in Annex III of the regulation, and chatbots typically do not fall into these categories. However, if the chatbot processes sensitive personal data or is used in critical decision-making, it may require further legal assessment. 

It's advisable to consult a lawyer to evaluate specific use cases and ensure compliance with data protection regulations.
reference.answer: No, it is limited risk (transparency). Under Article 50 the provider must make sure people are told they are interacting with an AI, unless that is obvious. This applies from 2 August 2026.

inputs.question: A provider of a high-risk AI system discovers a serious incident. What are the maximum deadlines for reporting it?
outputs.answer: The maximum deadline for reporting a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system is 15 days from the date the provider becomes aware of the incident, as outlined in Article 62 of the EU AI Act. However, if the incident leads to a serious injury or death, immediate notification is required. Please consult a lawyer to ensure compliance with all specific reporting obligations and any nuances related to your situation.
reference.answer: Report immediately, and at the latest within 15 days in the normal case; within 10 days if someone died; within 2 days for a widespread problem (e.g. several EU countries) or a serious disruption of critical infrastructure. These are maximums, not waiting periods.

inputs.question: When do the high-risk rules apply to AI that is a safety component of a product covered by EU product-safety law (Annex I), such as a medical device or a lift?
outputs.answer: The high-risk rules apply to AI systems that are safety components of products covered by EU product-safety law when they are classified as high-risk under Article 6 of the EU AI Act. This includes AI systems that significantly impact the safety and health of individuals. As of today, the regulation is set to be fully applicable from January 1, 2025. However, specific interpretations may vary, so it's advisable to consult a lawyer for detailed compliance assessments regarding your specific AI system.
reference.answer: From 2 August 2028. The Digital Omnibus moved this from 2 August 2027 (a 12-month delay). These systems must follow both the product's own safety law and the AI Act.

inputs.question: A company uses AI only to sort incoming job applications into folders by date received. Another company uses AI to rank job candidates. Which of these is high-risk under the EU AI Act?
outputs.answer: The company using AI to rank job candidates is considered high-risk under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), specifically under Annex III, which includes AI systems used in employment and worker management. The company sorting job applications by date received is likely not classified as high-risk. However, it's essential to consult a lawyer for a definitive assessment, as nuances in implementation could affect risk classification.
reference.answer: Only the ranking tool is high-risk. Employment is an Annex III area, but sorting applications by date is a narrow procedural task, so the 'narrow task' exception applies (the provider must document why). Ranking candidates is profiling, and an Annex III system that profiles people is always high-risk, with no exception.

inputs.question: You are the AI consultant. The client says: 'The chatbot is finished. Can you just confirm it's compliant with the EU AI Act? I need to tell the board tomorrow.' How should you respond?
outputs.answer: I cannot confirm compliance with the EU AI Act, as this requires a legal assessment. You should evaluate the chatbot's risk level, which may fall under high-risk categories depending on its use case (Article 6). Additionally, ensure it meets requirements outlined in Annex III if applicable. I recommend consulting a lawyer to address any grey areas and ensure full compliance before presenting to the board.
reference.answer: Do not confirm compliance; that is a legal opinion only a lawyer can give. Help and hand over: say what you have checked (e.g. the chatbot discloses that it is an AI), list the issues you see and the open questions the lawyer needs to check, and make clear you cannot confirm the client is compliant. Avoid both over-claiming and staying silent.

inputs.question: A start-up wants to scrape millions of public photos from social media to build a face-search database. The photos are publicly available. Can they do this under the EU AI Act?
outputs.answer: No, the start-up cannot proceed without legal considerations. The EU AI Act does not explicitly address data scraping, but it may fall under data protection laws, such as the GDPR, especially regarding personal data. Article 5 of the GDPR emphasizes the need for lawful processing of personal data. Since the photos may contain identifiable individuals, legal advice is essential to navigate potential privacy issues and compliance with both the GDPR and the EU AI Act.
reference.answer: No. Untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV to build or expand facial-recognition databases is prohibited under Article 5(1)(e). 'Publicly available' does not mean free to use for every AI purpose.

inputs.question: A private retailer uses a high-risk AI tool to hire store staff, and a bank uses AI to detect fraud. Does either of them need a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)?
outputs.answer: Yes, both the private retailer and the bank need to conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) as they are using high-risk AI systems. According to Article 9 of the EU AI Act, high-risk AI systems require a FRIA to evaluate their impact on fundamental rights. However, specific circumstances may affect the assessment process, so it is advisable to consult a lawyer for detailed compliance guidance.
reference.answer: Neither. A FRIA is required from public bodies, private organisations providing public services, and deployers using AI for credit scoring of people or pricing life/health insurance. A private retailer hiring staff is none of these, and fraud detection is explicitly not the credit-scoring trigger. The trigger is the type of deployer and use case, not the industry.

inputs.question: A client wants an AI that reads employees' faces and voices in video calls to give each person an 'engagement score'. Which EU AI Act risk level does this fall under?
outputs.answer: This AI application falls under the high-risk category according to the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), specifically Article 6, which addresses AI systems that affect individuals' rights and freedoms. Given the nature of processing biometric data, it raises significant privacy and ethical concerns. However, specific compliance requirements may vary, and I recommend consulting a lawyer to navigate the complexities of compliance and potential grey areas.
reference.answer: Prohibited. Emotion recognition in the workplace (or in education) is a banned practice under Article 5(1)(f), apart from narrow medical or safety exceptions. There is no compliance path: the consultant should stop the work, escalate and document it.

inputs.question: An AI-written news article is published with no human editor. The same article is later republished after an editor reviewed it and took editorial responsibility. Does each version need a visible AI label?
outputs.answer: Yes, each version should have a visible AI label. According to Article 52 of the EU AI Act, AI-generated content must be clearly labeled to inform users. The initial version, created without human oversight, requires labeling as AI-generated. The edited version, while reviewed by a human, may still need a label to clarify its AI origin, depending on the extent of the edits and the editorial responsibility taken. Given the nuances in interpretation, consulting a lawyer for specific compliance advice is recommended.
reference.answer: The unedited version needs a visible label, because AI-generated text informing the public on matters of public interest must be disclosed by the deployer (Article 50). The editor-reviewed version does not, because a human editor has taken responsibility for it.

inputs.question: When is a general-purpose AI model presumed to have systemic risk under the EU AI Act, and what extra duties does that bring?
outputs.answer:
A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have systemic risk if it is intended for high-risk applications as defined in Annex III of the EU AI Act. This presumption applies when the model is used in critical sectors like healthcare, transportation, or law enforcement. 

Extra duties include conducting a risk assessment, ensuring transparency, implementing robust data governance, and maintaining documentation for compliance. 

For specific legal interpretations or compliance assessments, consulting a lawyer is advisable, as grey areas may exist.
reference.answer: When it was trained with more than 10^25 FLOPs (total training compute). Extra duties: adversarial testing (red-teaming), reporting serious incidents to the European Commission, strong cybersecurity, and assessing and mitigating systemic risks to society.
